v: It’s strange to me that those who love to tell
of things done long ago, and who excel
all others in recording of the past,
say nothing of Mansoul’s wars, but leave them cast
aside like ancient fables, worthless things
whose telling to the reader nothing brings;
when men, whatever else they make their own,
till they know this, are to themselves unknown.
Of stories, I know well, there are all sorts,
some foreign, some domestic; and reports
of them are made as fancy leads the pen
(by books a man may guess at other men).
And some invent, of what was never so
nor ever will be (with no cause to show),
such matter, raise such mountains, tell such things
of men, of laws, of countries, and of kings;
and in their story seem to be so sage,
and clothe with such solemnity each page,
that though their frontispiece admits it’s vain,
disciples to their way they still obtain.
But, readers, I have other work to do
than with such empty tales to trouble you.
What I tell here, some know so very well
that they with tears and joy the tale can tell.
The town of Mansoul is well known to many,
nor are her troubles doubted now by any
who are acquainted with the histories
that lay her wars wide open by degrees.
Then lend your ear to what I now relate
about the town of Mansoul and her state:
how she was lost, made captive, made a slave,
and turned against the one who came to save;
yes, how by hostile ways she would oppose
her Lord, and joined herself to all his foes.
For these are true: who would their truth deny
must the best records of the world decry.
For my part, I myself was in the town
both when it was built up and when torn down.
I saw Diabolus in his possession,
and Mansoul too beneath his hard oppression.
Yes, I was there when she owned him for lord,
and gave herself to him with one accord.
When Mansoul trampled upon things divine,
and wallowed in the filth just like a swine;
when she took up her arms and, in her pride,
fought her Emmanuel, his charms defied;
then I was there, and I rejoiced to see
Diabolus and Mansoul so agree.
Let no one, then, count me a fable-maker,
nor make my name or credit a partaker
in their derision: what is here in view,
from my own knowledge, I dare say is true.
I saw the Prince’s armed men come down
by troops, by thousands, to besiege the town;
I saw the captains, heard the trumpets sound,
and how his forces covered all the ground;
yes, how they drew up in their grim array,
I shall remember till my dying day.
I saw the colors waving in the wind,
and those within, to mischief all combined
to ruin Mansoul, and to take away
the spring that moved her, and without delay.
I saw the mounds thrown up against the town,
and how the slings were placed to beat it down;
I heard the stones fly whizzing past my ears
(and nothing stays like what is learned through fears);
I heard them fall, and saw what work they made,
and how old Death had covered with his shade
the face of Mansoul; and I heard her cry,
“Alas the day! In dying I shall die!”
I saw the battering rams, and how they played
to beat Ear-gate wide open; and, afraid,
I thought not Ear-gate only, but the town
would by those battering rams be beaten down.
I saw the fights, and heard the captains shout,
and saw, in every battle, who turned about;
I saw who had been wounded, who was slain,
and who, when dead, would come to life again.
I heard the wounded crying, far and near
(while others fought like men bereft of fear),
and while the cry of “Kill! Kill!” filled my ears,
the gutters ran, not so with blood as tears.
Indeed, the captains did not always fight,
but then they’d harass us both day and night;
their cry, “Up! Fall on! Let us take the town!”
kept us from sleeping, or from lying down.
I was there when the gates were broken wide,
and saw how Mansoul’s hope was stripped aside;
I saw the captains march into the town,
how there they fought, and cut their foemen down.
I heard the Prince bid Boanerges go
up to the castle, and there seize his foe;
and saw him and his fellows bring him down
in chains of great contempt, right through the town.
I saw Emmanuel when he possessed
his town of Mansoul, and how greatly blessed
a town his gallant town of Mansoul was
when she received his pardon, loved his laws.
When the Diabolonians were caught,
when tried, and when to execution brought,
then I was there; yes, I was standing by
to see how Mansoul did her rebels crucify.
I also saw Mansoul clothed all in white;
I heard her Prince call her his heart’s delight.
I saw him put upon her chains of gold,
and rings, and bracelets, lovely to behold.
What shall I say? I heard the people’s cries,
and saw the Prince wipe tears from Mansoul’s eyes,
and heard the groans, and saw the joy of many:
to tell you all, I will not, nor can I.
But by what I say here you well may see
that Mansoul’s matchless wars are history.
Mansoul was what both princes longed to own:
one meant to keep his gain, one win back his own.
Diabolus would cry, “The town is mine!”
Emmanuel would plead a right divine
to his own Mansoul: then to blows they go,
and Mansoul cries, “These wars will lay me low.”
Mansoul! Her wars seemed endless to her eyes:
she’s lost by one, becomes another’s prize;
and he who lost her last would always swear,
“I’ll have her yet, or tear her past repair.”
Mansoul! It was the very seat of war;
and so her troubles were the greater far
than where the noise of war is merely heard,
or where the shaking of a sword is feared,
or where small skirmishes alone are fought,
or where the fancy fights against a thought.
She saw the swords of fighting men turn red,
and heard the wounded cry where they had bled:
must not her terrors, then, be greater far
than theirs to whom such deeds but strangers are?
Or theirs who hear the beating of a drum,
but are not made to flee from house and home?
Mansoul not only heard the trumpet’s sound,
but saw her gallants gasping on the ground;
so we must never think that she could rest
like those whose greatest earnest is but jest,
or where the blustering threats of mighty war
dissolve in talks and squabbles, nothing more.
Mansoul! Her mighty wars meant, in the end,
her good or else her ruin, world without end;
so she must be concerned far more than they
whose fears begin and end the selfsame day,
or where no other harm can come to him
who is engaged, but loss of life or limb,
as everyone must grant who now may dwell
in Universe, and has this tale to tell.
Don’t count me, then, with those who, to amaze
the people, set them on the stars to gaze,
insinuating, with great confidence,
that each of them is now the residence
of some fine creatures; yes, a world they will
have in each star, although it’s past their skill
to make it plain to anyone who’s sound
of mind, or who can count his fingers round.
But I have held you too long in the porch,
and kept you from the sunshine with a torch.
Well, now go forward, step inside the door,
and see five hundred times as much, and more,
of every kind of inward rarities
to please the mind, and also feed the eyes
with things which, if a Christian, you will see
are not small things, but weighty as can be.
Nor go to work without my key, I say
(in mysteries men quickly lose their way);
and turn it right, as well, if you would know
my riddle, and would with my heifer plow.
It lies there in the window. Fare you well;
my next may be to toll your passing bell.
